definition: A short, often amusing story about a real person or event.
example: Grandpa told an anecdote about the summer he worked on a fishing boat.
nuance: An anecdote is a brief real-life story, not an antidote (a cure for poison), and it counts as weaker evidence than data.
prompt: A guest speaker is opening her speech at a graduation ceremony.
options: She began with an anecdote about getting lost on her first day of college.
Before speaking, she swallowed an anecdote to soothe her sore throat.
Her anecdote was a full-length novel she read aloud for three hours.
Her anecdote was a chart of graduation rates from the past twenty years, shown on the big screen.
reasons: A brief true story from her own life is exactly this kind of story.
This confuses the word with antidote; a story is not something you swallow as a remedy.
An anecdote is short; a three-hour novel is far too long to count as one.
A chart of numbers is data, not a story about a person or event.

practice.prompt: A student is writing a persuasive essay about school lunches.
options: Maya opened with an anecdote about the day the cafeteria ran out of bread.
The anecdote in her table showed that 62 percent of students skip lunch.
After drinking spoiled milk, a classmate needed an anecdote from the school nurse.
Her anecdote was a single word, "delicious," written at the top of the page.
reasons: A short true story about one specific day is a fitting way to grab attention.
A percentage in a table is a statistic, not a story.
This mixes the word up with antidote, which treats poisoning; stories don't cure illness.
One word tells no story, so it cannot be an anecdote.
